newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK GOVT TO SUPPORT TIGHT C.BANK MONEY POLICY.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK GOVT TO SUPPORT TIGHT C.BANK MONEY POLICY.

text.p: Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik on Thursday said the government will support the central bank's tight monetary policy by maintaining the current ratio between real wages and labour productivity.

"We want to limit domestic demand for consumer goods by maintaining the current ratio between real wages and the productivity of labour which we consider appropriate," Kozlik told Reuters after addressing an economic conference.
"The central bank money supply policy towards banks and our maintenance of the wage and productivity ratio are the two basic demand-tightening instruments which will function next year," Kozlik said.
He added that the process would be "incredibly complicated" but did not elaborate.
The real wage index in Slovakia rose 5.7 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 1996, after a 3.4 percent increase in the same period in 1995.
Meanwhile labour productivity in the second quarter edged up 2.5 percent after a 5.5 percent gain in the first quarter.
Kozlik said the country's increased consumption, rather than ailing exports, could have prompted a crown devaluation, but recent central measures eased the pressure.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) said it has yet to review a series of measures it implemented two months ago to curb short-term lending, which is at the heart of the country's burgeoning money supply.

The NBS has also expressed concern whether loans which have entered the economy are being fully-utilised for industrial reform, and warned that if this were not so it could negatively affect the balance of payments in the future.
The NBS measures included a hike in bank minimum reserve levels, a hike in the Lombard last-resort lending facility, and widening the band in which it fixes the crown.
The Slovak key money supply measure, M2, rose 19.5 percent year-on-year in August, after a 21.0 percent year-on-year expansion in July.

"Our aim is manageable support for healthy non- inflationary (long-term) economic growth mainly by using internal reserves and decreasing state budget deficits and aiming for a balanced budget," Kozlik said.
He said the government also intended to support in the "longer-term" exports and inflow of mainly direct foreign capital, though he did not elaborate further.
Many Slovak groups have called for the government to help support exports, though any controls on wages are expected to be met with disdain.

Slovak inflation rose 5.2 percent year-on-year in September after a 5.5 percent rise in August. The current account deficit hit $847.2 million in the first seven months of 1996, after a surplus of $488.5 million in the same period of 1995.
